name: Erbium YAG resurfacing

lead: Er:YAG resurfacing removes thin layers of skin to smooth acne scars, deep wrinkles and pigment such as melasma. It is described as a gentler-heat alternative to CO2.

The 2940 nm beam is strongly absorbed by water and ablates shallow layers with limited heat spreading into surrounding tissue. Wikipedia says this gives a lower risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than CO2. Much of the early Er:YAG research concerns dental tissue; skin trials in the sources are small registrations covering skin aging, acne scars with PRP and cutaneous neurofibromas.

paras: It is done in a clinic, in one session or a short series depending on the depth wanted. Skin typically looks pink and peels while it heals, with a recovery that depends on settings. It is sometimes combined with other treatments for acne scars.

Reported risks of laser resurfacing include scarring, pigment change, acne and herpes outbreaks. Redness, swelling and peeling are expected during healing. People prone to cold sores, scarring or pigment changes should discuss this with the provider.

chain: Skin heals with less heat damage
Smoother texture, fewer scars and wrinkles
angle.text: Er:YAG removes thin layers of skin with a water-absorbing laser, so skin heals with less heat damage and ends up smoother, with fewer scars and wrinkles. It is used for acne scars, deep wrinkles and melasma, and is described as shallower than CO2.

lead: Erbium:YAG (Er:YAG) resurfacing uses a 2940 nm infrared laser to remove thin layers of skin, and people use it to smooth acne scars, soften deep wrinkles, even out sun damage and treat melasma, giving the face a smoother, more uniform surface [1][2]. The wavelength is strongly absorbed by water in tissue, so the beam acts shallowly, which is why the technique is often described as a gentler-heat alternative to the CO2 laser [1][2].

Er:YAG light can be delivered across the whole treated area (fully ablative) or as a grid of microscopic columns that leaves untreated skin between them (ablative fractional), the second approach having been introduced in 2007 and cleared by the US FDA for wrinkles, rhytides, fine lines, textural irregularities, pigmented lesions and vascular dyschromia [3]. Heating and controlled injury in the dermis prompt new collagen and elastin formation, which is how the treatment is meant to improve texture over the weeks after it [2].

The 2940 nm laser has a long research history outside skin: early 1989 laboratory work examined it on teeth and bone, and it is now used in dentistry, periodontology and oral surgery [4][5][6]. In skin, systematic reviews have compared ablative fractional erbium and CO2 lasers with needling for scars, and meta-analyses have pooled laser treatments for melasma [7][8]. Reported complications of resurfacing in general include scarring, pigment change, acne flares and herpes outbreaks [2].

paras: Er:YAG resurfacing is used for skin appearance problems that sit in the upper layers of the skin: acne scarring, deep rhytides (wrinkles), solar damage and age spots, and melasma [1][2]. Laser resurfacing as a family is also applied to surgical scars, stretch marks, actinic keratosis and telangiectasias [2]. A 2019 review of stretch-mark treatments lists Er:YAG among the lasers that have been tried, alongside CO2, diode, Q-switched Nd:YAG, pulsed dye and excimer systems [9]. The 2940 nm wavelength is also used to cut bone and soft tissue in oral and maxillofacial surgery and in dentistry, where it removes decay with less vibration than a drill [1].

For many people the aim is textural: shallower acne-scar edges, finer lines around the eyes and mouth, and a more even tone. Practitioners describe fully ablative erbium as a resurfacing peel in a beam, in which the epidermis and part of the dermis are vaporised and the skin regrows smoother [2]. Fractional erbium treats only a portion of the skin surface at a time, leaving up to about 95 percent of it untouched so that the surrounding tissue can repair the epidermis quickly [3].

The laser disrupts molecular bonds in the skin's water-rich tissue, vaporising it; heat in the deeper dermis then stimulates fibroblasts to lay down new collagen and elastin, which is credited with improving turgor and thickness [2]. Because erbium light is absorbed far more strongly by water than CO2 light is, it removes tissue in thin, precise layers and leaves less residual heat in the tissue below [1][2]. A 1989 laboratory study measured 10 to 50 microns of residual collagen damage with ordinary pulses at the walls of Er:YAG incisions, a figure often cited to explain the smaller coagulation zone [10]. Wikipedia attributes the lower hypopigmentation and scarring risk of erbium, relative to CO2, to this lower heat and coagulation [2].

Wikipedia's laser-resurfacing entry groups lasers by how they treat the skin: ablative devices such as Er:YAG and CO2 vaporise tissue and create a controlled wound, non-ablative devices (for example the 1540 nm erbium:glass laser) keep the surface intact, and fractional devices deliver light as many tiny points with healthy skin left between them [2]. Some studies cited there found direct heat can cause DNA damage in treated and nearby cells, and the entry says further research is warranted [2].

Non-ablative lasers keep the skin surface intact, ablative lasers such as Er:YAG and CO2 vaporise tissue and create a wound, and fractional lasers deliver light as many tiny points [2]. Non-ablative fractional photothermolysis arrived on the market in 2003; the ablative fractional concept, using Er:YAG or CO2 light, followed in 2007 [3]. Fractional approaches were developed as a route to effective resurfacing with a lower risk profile and quicker epidermal repair than fully ablative work [3].

Reported complications of laser resurfacing include scarring, hyperpigmentation, acne and herpes outbreaks [2]. A 2008 study of 961 fractional laser treatments recorded acne and herpes flares, and anecdotal accounts describe scarring and pigment change [2]. Wikipedia states that CO2 lasers carry a higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers [2]. Ablative lasers by definition create a wound in the skin, which is why complications of this kind are discussed in reviews of laser resurfacing [11].

Fully ablative erbium treats the whole surface of an area and is described as a resurfacing peel in a beam [2]. Ablative fractional erbium treats only a portion of the surface at a time, with up to about 95 percent left untouched in some settings, and the US FDA has cleared ablative fractional Er:YAG devices for wrinkles, fine lines, textural irregularities, pigmented lesions and vascular dyschromia [3]. Erbium is also combined with other approaches: a registered trial combines lasers with platelet-rich plasma for post-acne scars [12].

Er:YAG light is not only used on the face. Wikipedia lists wart removal, where a 1998 study found HPV DNA was not detected in the plume, as another use, and notes cataract surgery is possible though Nd:YAG lasers are preferred [1]. Registrations also cover neurofibroma vaporisation [13] and intimate-area treatments [14].

Evidence for Er:YAG on skin comes from reviews of several lasers together and from small registered trials. A 2023 systematic review of ten articles compared needling (radiofrequency, meso- and micro-needling) with ablative fractional lasers (CO2 and erbium) for atrophic and hypertrophic scars; in 60 percent of the studies there was no statistically significant difference between the two approaches, and both produced significant improvement [7].

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of laser treatment for melasma pooled 22 studies with 694 patients and found that most lasers and laser combinations, including fractional ablative CO2, were associated with reduced MASI scores, while noting indeterminate results across trials [8]. A 2019 review of stretch-mark treatment likewise lists Er:YAG among many options used with variable success and a limited quality of evidence [9].

Registered trials include a 151-person study from 2007 evaluating the safety and efficacy of erbium treatment for skin aging [15], a 21-person study of epidermal delivery of anti-aging ingredients for wrinkles, acne scars and pigmentation [16], a 32-person trial combining lasers with platelet-rich plasma for post-acne scars [12] and a 12-person phase 2/3 study of Er:YAG vaporisation of cutaneous neurofibromas [13]. A sham-controlled trial of 136 women compared Er:YAG with a CO2RE intimate laser for vaginal atrophy [14]. Results for these registrations are not posted in the registry entries cited here.

Outside skin, randomized trials have used Er:YAG in dentistry, for example as an adjunct in periodontal pocket therapy, peri-implantitis surgery and frenectomy, and a meta-analysis of peri-implantitis protocols found no added effect of Er:YAG on probing pocket depth reduction [17][18].

Er:YAG output at 2940 nm was characterised in tissue in the late 1980s: 1989 papers measured ablation rates on dental enamel and dentin, described minimal damage to surrounding tissue under the microscope, and quantified thermal damage in skin, cornea, aorta and bone [4][5][10]. Laser resurfacing itself began with CO2 lasers; Thomas L. Roberts III is credited with developing the technique in the 1990s and presented it in 1995, then co-authored a 1996 paper on recognising and minimising complications [2]. Erbium systems and fractional delivery followed, with ablative fractional Er:YAG introduced in 2007 [3].

Er:YAG resurfacing sits in the clinic-based part of appearance improvement: it is performed by physicians and trained practitioners rather than at home, and is discussed among people comparing resurfacing options for scars and aging skin. Comparisons with CO2 lasers, radiofrequency needling and microneedling are common, and the Er:YAG laser is also widely known from dentistry [1][7].

Among people comparing options, erbium is usually placed between lighter treatments such as chemical peels, microneedling and non-ablative lasers and deeper CO2 resurfacing. Reviews of facial rejuvenation compare five widely used methods: CO2 laser, Er:YAG laser, combination resurfacing, fractional photothermolysis and plasma resurfacing [11]. A 2010 review by Bogdan Allemann and Kaufman describes how non-ablative fractional treatment (introduced in 2003) and ablative fractional treatment (introduced in 2007 with Er:YAG or CO2) leave most skin untouched, which supports faster epidermal repair [3].

lore.intro: Erbium resurfacing is discussed mainly by clinicians and in reference sources rather than DIY forums, with recurring claims about gentler heat, shorter recovery and scar results [1][2][3].
